title: Rate limiting for the Orders API
subtitle: feature/rate-limit → main

scenes.narration: This change does three things to the orders API. It stops one visitor from flooding the API with requests. It prices each order with real prices. And it announces every new order to other services. There are no tests, so the code needs a careful read.
scenes.summary: Add Redis-backed rate limiting to POST /orders and publish order.created events.
bullets: A Redis outage now **fails every order request**, because the limiter has no fallback
`publish` runs after the insert, so a queue outage returns an error for an order that was saved
No tests cover the limiter, the pricing lookup, or the new event

scenes.narration: Here are the parts involved. The new piece is a rate limiter, which caps how many requests one visitor can send.

steps.say: The limiter keeps its counts in Redis, a shared in-memory store, so every server sees the same numbers.
The limiter does not handle a Redis outage. If Redis is down, the limiter fails, and so does every order.
The orders service, the code that saves orders, now asks the pricing module for prices before it writes to the database.
The event queue is also new. Other services read the queue to learn about new orders.

scenes.title: POST /orders
scenes.narration: Here is the order of calls for one order request.

steps.say: The request reaches the rate limiter first. The limiter asks Redis to add one to this visitor's count.
Then the orders service gets the prices and saves the order.
After the save, the API puts an order created message on the queue. The API waits until the queue accepts the message, not until another service acts on it. Then the API answers the client.

scenes.title: POST /orders
scenes.narration: Now follow the data. The client sends a user and a list of items. The limiter turns the visitor's IP address into a count of requests this minute. The saved order comes back with a total and a pending status. The message to the queue carries only the order's id and total.

scenes.title: orders
scenes.narration: The orders table changes in two ways.

steps.say: The orders table gets a new status column. Every new order starts as pending.
The order total now comes from the pricing module, not from what the client sent.
Each order still belongs to one user, and still has many items.

scenes.narration: The rate limiter counts each visitor's requests in the current minute, by IP address. The count starts again at zero every new minute, because Redis deletes the count when the minute ends. Past twenty requests, the limiter answers with a too many requests error, and says when to try again. Otherwise the request goes on.
scenes.calloutText: Expiry is set once per window, so the key cleans itself up.

flow.label: Count this request in the IP's one-minute window
On the first hit, expire the key with the window
Over the limit? Refuse the request
flow.outcome: Past twenty: too many requests, with Retry-After

flow.label: Under the limit, pass the request on

scenes.narration: The API puts the rate limiter in front of the orders route, the address clients send new orders to. The API also announces each order after the order is saved.

steps.say: The limiter allows each visitor twenty requests in every one-minute window.
After the order is saved, the route sends the order created message, and waits until the queue accepts the message.

scenes.calloutText: publish runs after the insert, so a queue outage fails the request.

scenes.narration: The order total used to price every item at ten. Now the orders service asks the pricing module for each item's real price. The service looks up all the prices at once, instead of one after another. An order with no items is refused before anything is saved.
scenes.calloutText: Pricing lookups run in parallel with Promise.all.

scenes.title: Test coverage
scenes.subject: rateLimit, createOrder and the orders route
scenes.narration: This change adds no tests. Nothing checks that a visitor's requests after the first twenty in a minute are refused. Nothing checks what happens when Redis or the queue is down. And nothing checks that an empty order is refused.

Empty orders are rejected and totals use prices from the pricing service
